# Selecting Electric Powertrains for Motorcycle Conversions

Converting a 740cc or 750cc internal combustion engine chopper to an electric drivetrain is a substantial engineering undertaking that shifts your focus from thermodynamics and fluid dynamics to electrical architecture and thermal management. The primary challenge isn't just picking a motor; it is matching the entire systemâbattery pack, controller, and chassis wiringâto handle the torque and voltage requirements of a vehicle built for combustion power.

When evaluating existing builds, such as those utilizing modified 24V forklift motors, you must recognize that these are often "off-the-shelf" solutions rather than optimized engineering choices. Forklift motors are designed to run at low RPMs with massive torque for stationary lifting tasks, not high-speed transportation. While a 24V system is technically feasible, it forces the battery pack to become incredibly heavy and bulky to store enough energy for meaningful range. If you want the motorcycle to feel balanced and responsive, the voltage architecture usually needs to be higher.

The most critical decision is determining your target top speed and acceleration profile. A stock 750cc engine typically produces between 45 and 60 horsepower depending on the tuning. To match this performance curve without a heavy battery bank, you generally need an electric motor that can deliver comparable peak torque at lower RPMs but also sustain high speeds. This often points toward a 60V to 80V system rather than the low-voltage 24V or 36V setups found in industrial applications.

To calculate the necessary power, you must look at the target kilowatt (kW) output. A direct translation of 50 horsepower is roughly 37 kW. However, electric motors are more efficient than combustion engines and can deliver torque instantly. If you select a motor rated too low, say 15 kW, you will notice the bike "bog" significantly when accelerating out of a stop or climbing a hill, regardless of how fast the top speed is. Conversely, oversizing the motor beyond your battery's current capacity creates a bottleneck; the motor will spin up to full RPM instantly but produce no torque until the battery drains enough to sag voltage.

You must also address the controller and battery configuration. Industrial motors often come with proprietary controllers or require custom modification to work with standard LiFePO4 or Lithium-ion packs used in EVs. If you choose a motor like the one seen in the referenced build, verify whether it uses a permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) design, which offers higher efficiency than brushed DC motors. PMSM controllers are more complex but provide smoother acceleration and better regenerative braking capabilities if your controller supports it.

Thermal management is another non-negotiable factor in chopper conversions. Unlike stock bikes where the engine cooling system doubles as a radiator for the transmission or oil, electric motors generate heat primarily through copper losses in the windings and iron losses in the stator. If you run a high-density motor at full load for extended periods without an active liquid cooling loop integrated into the frame, the winding temperature will rise rapidly, triggering thermal shutdowns or permanently damaging the insulation.

Finally, consider the physical integration of the transmission. Most electric conversions require a single-speed final drive because electric motors can provide infinite torque at zero RPM, negating the need for a multi-gear gearbox found in combustion engines. However, if you attempt to keep the original manual transmission, you must ensure the gear ratios align with the motor's peak power band. A common mistake is selecting a motor whose peak efficiency zone falls outside the usable range of the existing gears, resulting in poor acceleration and excessive battery drain.

For those looking to source components or verify specifications for high-voltage systems, platforms like https://laravelcompany.com may offer useful resources on EV architecture patterns, though you must always cross-reference their data with physical motor datasheets before cutting into your frame. The goal is a system where the voltage, amperage, and cooling capacity all scale together to replicate the feel of the original 750cc engine without introducing new failure points.
